goals: Create useful features from raw columns
Know when each encoding is appropriate
why: Better features usually beat fancier algorithms. Many Kaggle winners credit feature engineering, not model choice, for their edge.
explain: Models only see numbers. **Feature engineering** turns raw data into numbers that expose the pattern: ratios (debt ÷ income), differences (days since last purchase), date parts (month, weekday) and aggregates (average spend over the last 90 days).
**One-hot encoding** turns a category with k values into k columns of 0/1. Use it for unordered categories such as city.
**Ordinal encoding** maps ordered categories to numbers (small = 1, medium = 2, large = 3). Do **not** use it for unordered categories: it would imply Chennai < Mumbai < Pune.

**Target encoding** replaces a category with the average target for that category. It is powerful for high-cardinality columns (10,000 product IDs) but must be computed inside cross-validation to avoid leakage.

example.title: Credit features
steps: Raw: income ₹10L, existing EMIs ₹4L per year
City = Pune → one-hot: is_chennai 0, is_pune 1, is_mumbai 0
example.result: Debt-to-income is often a far stronger predictor than income or EMIs alone.

mistakes: Target encoding on the full dataset (leakage).
Creating features that use future information.
takeaways: Ratios, differences, dates and aggregates expose patterns
One-hot for unordered categories, ordinal for ordered ones
Domain knowledge is the best feature generator

practice.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"income": [10, 20], "emi": [4, 2], "city": ["Pune", "Chennai"],
                   "applied": pd.to_datetime(["2026-03-14", "2026-03-15"])})
df["dti"] = df.emi / df.income
df["weekday"] = df.applied.dt.weekday
df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["city"])
print(df)
